metadata.title: School belonging and math attitudes among high school students in advanced math

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TIMSS 2015 Advanced Mathematics data, where students are sampled via a two-stage stratified cluster design (random schools, then intact classes). The authors state that supplied student-level sampling weights were used and that standard errors were adjusted for the complex multi-stage design using jackknife replications. Because the analysis is conducted separately by country/region, the weighting and jackknife approach is applied within each country’s analytic sample to reflect the survey’s clustering and stratification. The paper does not report a specific weight variable name (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly confirms that complex-survey weighting and jackknife replicate variance estimation were part of the regression estimation procedure.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables (SLM and SVM) are TIMSS scale scores computed using IRT, and the TIMSS math achievement covariate is based on five plausible values. The paper describes how plausible values were handled (five separate regressions with averaged parameter estimates), but it does not describe any explicit missing-data strategy for student background items or scale items. This is a reporting gap because missingness handling can affect regression coefficients and standard errors in survey-based analyses.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample consists of students in the TIMSS 2015 Advanced Mathematics population who were in the final year of secondary school and enrolled in one or more advanced science or mathematics courses. The TIMSS Advanced sample is drawn from advanced mathematics students using a two-stage stratified cluster sampling procedure: a random sample of schools followed by selection of one or two intact classes. The paper does not report additional exclusions beyond the TIMSS sampling/eligibility definition, and it does not specify further task-level filters for the attitude scales.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2015 Advanced Mathematics (final year secondary) — Students Like Learning Advanced Mathematics (SLM) scale
main_findings.performance_metrics: Country-wise multiple regression (jackknife SEs with sampling weights; 5 plausible values averaged). Reported model fit: R2 ranges by country/region (France 0.29, Italy 0.17, Lebanon 0.19, Norway 0.26, Portugal 0.28, Russian Federation 0.21, Slovenia 0.28, Sweden 0.29, U.S. 0.19). Relative importance (Pratt indices): math achievement is most important for SLM in most countries; sense of school belonging is most important in Lebanon (and is also the single most important predictor of SLM among Lebanese students per narrative).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2015 Advanced Mathematics the study leveraged sense of school belonging, TIMSS math achievement, parental education level, and gender (female vs male) to predict Students Like Learning Advanced Mathematics (SLM), finding that sense of school belonging was a statistically significant positive predictor of SLM in each of the nine countries/regions (each p < .001) while math achievement was the most important predictor for most countries. This indicates that strengthening students’ perceived belonging in advanced-math learning environments may be a key lever for improving students’ liking of advanced mathematics, though the correlational design limits causal claims.

main_findings.dataset_used: TIMSS 2015 Advanced Mathematics (final year secondary) — Students Value Advanced Mathematics (SVM) scale
main_findings.performance_metrics: Country-wise multiple regression (jackknife SEs with sampling weights; 5 plausible values averaged). Reported model fit: R2 ranges by country/region (France 0.19, Italy 0.13, Lebanon 0.15, Norway 0.09, Portugal 0.19, Russian Federation 0.16, Slovenia 0.18, Sweden 0.09, U.S. 0.09). Relative importance (Pratt indices): math achievement is most important for SVM in most countries; sense of school belonging is the single most important predictor of SVM in Italy, Lebanon, Norway, and Russia per narrative.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TIMSS 2015 Advanced Mathematics the study leveraged sense of school belonging, TIMSS math achievement, parental education level, and gender (female vs male) to predict Students Value Advanced Mathematics (SVM), finding that sense of school belonging was a statistically significant positive predictor of SVM in each of the nine countries/regions (each p < .001) and was the most important predictor in Italy, Lebanon, Norway, and Russia. This indicates that improving school climate and students’ sense of acceptance/respect in advanced-math tracks may increase students’ perceived value of mathematics, though causality cannot be inferred from the regression results.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes TIMSS 2015 Advanced Mathematics data for students in the final year of secondary school enrolled in advanced mathematics/science courses across nine countries/regions (France, Italy, Lebanon, Norway, Portugal, Russian Federation, Slovenia, Sweden, and the U.S.). It predicts two TIMSS attitude scales—Students Like Learning Advanced Mathematics (SLM) and Students Value Advanced Mathematics (SVM)—using multiple regression with sampling weights and jackknife replicate-based standard errors, while handling the TIMSS math achievement covariate via five plausible values (five regressions with averaged parameter estimates). Across all countries, students’ sense of school belonging is a statistically significant positive predictor of both SLM and SVM (each p < .001), with math achievement often the most important predictor by Pratt indices, except where belonging dominates (e.g., SVM in Italy, Lebanon, Norway, Russia). Gender shows significant main effects in some countries and limited moderation overall. Limitations include reliance on self-reported attitudes and a correlational design, so significant predictors should not be interpreted as causal effects.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This paper is an empirical regression study using TIMSS survey data (weighted multiple regression with jackknife SEs and plausible-value averaging), not a machine-learning predictive modeling study. As a result, no ML algorithms are evaluated (ml_techniques.all_techniques is empty), and the extraction focuses on regression-based associations rather than ML performance metrics such as AUC or RMSE. The presence of R2 and Pratt indices reflects traditional model fit and relative importance, not ML model selection.
